Minimally Invasive Steering of Language Models

Taha Entesari    Jingyu Zhang    Daniel Khashabi    Mahyar Fazlyab Affiliation: Johns Hopkins University
Abstract

Pre-logit steering adapts a frozen language model to a test-time reward by adding vectors to its final hidden states. Unregularized reward optimization can substantially alter the output distribution and degrade generation quality. We propose Minimally Invasive Steering Vector Optimization (MISVO), which penalizes interventions using the local KL geometry of the induced token distribution. The resulting Fisher quadratic measures distributional sensitivity and admits an analytic gradient computed through matrix–vector products with the frozen language-model head. We derive an exact decomposition of the sequence-level KL gradient into an analytic Fisher term and a suffix score-function term. For a fixed generation horizon, we show that the suffix term is second order in the steering magnitude and that three Fisher surrogates agree with the full KL gradient to first order. MISVO uses the frozen-reference surrogate to optimize position-specific interventions without updating model parameters. Across preference and code-generation tasks on models with approximately 1B–14B parameters, MISVO achieves the highest mean reward in six of seven model–task settings, with diversity and coherence scores close to those of Best-of-NN.

1 Introduction

Post-training methods, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback [34], align large language models (LLMs) by updating their parameters. At deployment, however, the target reward may depend on the user or context, change over time, or be available only through a black-box evaluator. Test-time alignment addresses these settings by adapting generation to the available reward while keeping model parameters fixed [21, 33, 22, 19, 45].

One approach to test-time alignment is activation steering, which modifies generation through additive interventions, or steering vectors, in the model’s hidden representations [38, 40]. These interventions can be fixed in advance or adapted during inference to the current prompt and target objective [22, 19]. In this paper, we focus on pre-logit steering, which applies interventions immediately before the language-model head [19]. This parameterization permits reward optimization without backpropagation through the transformer body. However, without sufficient regularization, optimization can push residual states far from the reachable manifold [32], leading to oversteering that degrades coherence or diversity. Optimizing an imperfect reward can also amplify these effects by favoring outputs that exploit the evaluator [16, 24].

To mitigate oversteering, we propose minimally invasive steering, which optimizes steering vectors at inference to balance reward improvement against deviation from the reference policy. Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence naturally measures this deviation by comparing the induced output distributions [34, 23, 18]. However, differentiating the sequence-level KL requires accounting for how steering changes the prefix distribution, introducing a score-function term whose Monte Carlo estimation can have high variance. This motivates a quadratic surrogate with an analytic gradient. An isotropic penalty on the squared Euclidean norm is computationally simple but ignores distributional sensitivity: equal-norm steering vectors can induce substantially different changes in token probabilities. We instead derive the quadratic penalty from the local KL geometry, yielding a Fisher-information cost matrix that captures the distributional sensitivity of each steering direction. Its gradient is computed through matrix–vector products with the frozen language-model head. We relate this gradient to the full sequence-level KL gradient, including the omitted score-function term, and establish first-order agreement near zero steering for a fixed generation horizon. The resulting algorithm, Minimally Invasive Steering Vector Optimization (MISVO), combines reward-gradient estimates with an analytic regularizer gradient and reuses a reference-policy Fisher estimate throughout test-time optimization. In summary, we make the following contributions:

  • •

    Distribution-sensitive steering. We formulate pre-logit steering as reward maximization with a quadratic effort penalty and derive the cost matrix from token-level KL geometry (Proposition 1). The associated quadratic form equals the variance of the induced logit perturbation.

  • •

    Sequence-level gradient analysis. We decompose the exact KL gradient into an analytic Fisher term and a suffix score-function term (Theorem 1). We bound the differences between three Fisher surrogates (Theorem 2) and establish that the suffix term is second order for a fixed horizon (Proposition 2). Thus, the frozen-Fisher gradient approximates the full KL gradient with error O⁡(‖u‖2)O(\|u\|^{2}) near the origin.

  • •

    Algorithm and evaluation. MISVO combines a score-function reward estimator with an analytic regularizer gradient (Algorithm 1). Experiments on SHP and MBPP+ evaluate reward, generation quality, distributional deviation, runtime, and memory across four frozen models with approximately 1B–14B parameters.

2 Problem Setup

Fix a prompt xx and a generation horizon TT. Let y=(y1,…,yT)y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{T}) denote a response over a vocabulary of size VV, and let ht=ht​(x,y<t)∈ℝdh_{t}=h_{t}(x,y_{<t})\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be the frozen model’s hidden state immediately before the language-model (LM) head. With head parameters W∈ℝV×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d} and b∈ℝVb\in\mathbb{R}^{V}, the reference policy is

πref(⋅∣x,y<t)=softmax(Wht+b),πref(y∣x)=∏t=1Tπref(yt∣x,y<t).\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})=\softmax(Wh_{t}+b),\qquad\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}).

An external evaluator assigns a terminal reward R⁡(x,y)∈ℝR(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}, which need not be differentiable.

Pre-logit steering.

For each prompt, we optimize position-specific vectors u=(u1,…,uT)∈ℝd×Tu=(u_{1},\dots,u_{T})\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times T}, shared across responses sampled under the current policy. The steered policy is

πu(⋅∣x,y<t)=softmax(W(ht+ut)+b),πu(y∣x)=∏t=1Tπu(yt∣x,y<t).\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})=\softmax\!\big(W(h_{t}+u_{t})+b\big),\qquad\pi_{u}(y\mid x)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{u}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}).

All model parameters remain fixed, and π0=πref\pi_{0}=\pi_{\text{ref}}. For a fixed prefix, ht​(x,y<t)h_{t}(x,y_{<t}) is independent of uu, and steering changes the logits by W​utWu_{t}. Gradients with respect to the steering vectors therefore require no backpropagation through the transformer body, although steering changes the distribution of sampled prefixes.

KL-regularized alignment.

A standard test-time alignment objective is [23, 22]

maxq(⋅∣x)𝔼y∼q[R(x,y)]−λKL(q(⋅∣x)∥πref(⋅∣x)),λ>0,\max_{q(\cdot\mid x)}\;\mathbb{E}_{y\sim q}[R(x,y)]-\lambda\,\KL\!\big(q(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)\big),\qquad\lambda>0,

where the maximization is over response distributions and λ\lambda controls the reward–deviation trade-off. Its unique optimizer is the ideal reward-tilted distribution

q⋆​(y∣x)=πref​(y∣x)​exp⁡(R⁡(x,y)/λ)∑y′πref​(y′∣x)​exp⁡(R⁡(x,y′)/λ).q^{\star}(y\mid x)=\frac{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp(R(x,y)/\lambda)}{\sum_{y^{\prime}}\pi_{\text{ref}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)\exp(R(x,y^{\prime})/\lambda)}.

Our goal is to approximate sampling from q⋆q^{\star} through pre-logit steering, while keeping all model parameters fixed.

3 Proposed Method: Minimally Invasive Steering

The ideal distribution q⋆q^{\star} need not be representable by position-specific pre-logit interventions. Restricting the KL-regularized objective to the steering policy class gives

maxu∈ℝd×T𝔼y∼πu(⋅∣x)[R(x,y)]−λKL(πu(⋅∣x)∥πref(⋅∣x)).\max_{u\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times T}}\;\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x)}[R(x,y)]-\lambda\,\KL\!\big(\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)\big). (1)

Equivalently, this problem minimizes KL(πu(⋅∣x)∥q⋆(⋅∣x))\KL(\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,q^{\star}(\cdot\mid x)) over the steering policy class. By the autoregressive chain rule, the sequence-level KL decomposes into expected token-level divergences:

ℰKL​(u)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{KL}}(u) :=KL(πu(⋅∣x)∥πref(⋅∣x))\displaystyle:=\KL\!\big(\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)\big) (2)
=∑t=1T𝔼y<t∼πu[KL(πu(⋅∣x,y<t)∥πref(⋅∣x,y<t))].\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim\pi_{u}}\!\left[\KL\!\big(\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\big)\right].

A derivation is provided in Appendix B.2. Although each token-level divergence can be evaluated directly, the prefix distribution also depends on uu. Differentiating this distribution contributes a score-function term whose Monte Carlo estimation can have high variance, motivating an alterntive regularizer.

Quadratic regularization.

We replace the KL penalty with a quadratic surrogate:

maxu∈ℝd×TJ(u):=𝔼y∼πu(⋅∣x)[R(x,y)]−λℰΣ(u),ℰΣ(u):=12∑t=1Tut⊤Σtut,\max_{u\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times T}}\quad J(u):=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x)}[R(x,y)]-\lambda\,\mathcal{E}_{\Sigma}(u),\qquad\mathcal{E}_{\Sigma}(u):=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}u_{t}^{\top}\Sigma_{t}u_{t}, (3)

where Σt∈ℝd×d\Sigma_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} are fixed symmetric positive semidefinite cost matrices. This gives the analytic gradient ∇utℰΣ​(u)=Σt​ut\nabla_{u_{t}}\mathcal{E}_{\Sigma}(u)=\Sigma_{t}u_{t}. We first present the resulting optimization algorithm, then derive a Fisher-based choice of Σt\Sigma_{t} from the local KL geometry in Section 4.

3.1 Algorithm

We optimize (3) by stochastic gradient ascent. At each iteration, we sample K>1K>1 independent responses y(i)∼πu(⋅∣x)y^{(i)}\sim\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x) and evaluate their rewards Ri=R⁡(x,y(i))R_{i}=R(x,y^{(i)}). The update direction at position tt is

gtR\displaystyle g_{t}^{R} :=1K​∑i=1K(Ri−R¯i)​W⊤​(eyt(i)−pt(i)),\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}(R_{i}-\bar{R}_{i})\,W^{\top}\big(e_{y_{t}^{(i)}}-p_{t}^{(i)}\big), (4)
dt\displaystyle d_{t} :=gtR−λΣtut,ut+:=ut+ηdt,\displaystyle:=g_{t}^{R}-\lambda\,\Sigma_{t}u_{t},\qquad u_{t}^{+}:=u_{t}+\eta d_{t},

where pt(i)=πu(⋅∣x,y<t(i))p_{t}^{(i)}=\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}^{(i)}) and eyt(i)∈ℝVe_{y_{t}^{(i)}}\in\mathbb{R}^{V} is the corresponding one-hot vector. The leave-one-out baseline R¯i=(K−1)−1​∑j≠iRj\bar{R}_{i}=(K-1)^{-1}\sum_{j\neq i}R_{j} reduces variance without biasing the reward-gradient estimator [3]. All positions are updated using rollouts and token probabilities from the same policy iterate. Algorithm 1 summarizes the procedure. It returns the final steered policy and the highest-reward response sampled during optimization.

4 Fisher Cost Matrices

In this section, we derive the cost matrices Σt\Sigma_{t} defined in (3) from the local geometry of KL divergence and quantify how closely the resulting regularizer gradient approximates the full sequence-level KL gradient.

4.1 From token-level KL to a quadratic penalty

Setting Σt=I\Sigma_{t}=I gives the isotropic penalty ℰΣ​(u)=12​∑t‖ut‖22\mathcal{E}_{\Sigma}(u)=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{t}\|u_{t}\|_{2}^{2}, which measures hidden-state displacement without accounting for its effect on token probabilities. To capture this distributional sensitivity, we use the classical information-geometric result that the Fisher information determines the second-order expansion of KL divergence [6, 7]. We then specialize this relation to additive pre-logit interventions to construct a quadratic steering penalty.

Specifically, fix a position tt and prefix y<ty_{<t}. Write z=W​ht+bz=Wh_{t}+b for the reference logits, δ=W​ut\delta=Wu_{t} for the steering-induced perturbation, and πut=πu(⋅∣x,y<t)\pi_{u}^{t}=\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}). The log-partition function A(z)=log∑i=1VeziA(z)=\log\sum_{i=1}^{V}e^{z_{i}} gives

KL(πut∥πreft)=A(z)−A(z+δ)+⟨πut,δ⟩.\KL(\pi_{u}^{t}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}^{t})=A(z)-A(z+\delta)+\langle\pi_{u}^{t},\delta\rangle. (5)

Moreover, its Hessian is given by

∇2A​(z)=diag⁡(πreft)−πreft​(πreft)⊤=:Cπreft.\nabla^{2}A(z)=\diag(\pi_{\text{ref}}^{t})-\pi_{\text{ref}}^{t}(\pi_{\text{ref}}^{t})^{\top}=:C_{\pi_{\text{ref}}^{t}}. (6)

We now expand this expression around ut=0u_{t}=0 to identify the desired quadratic form.

Proposition 1 (Token-level KL approximation with Fisher information matrix).

For a fixed prefix,

KL(πut∥πreft)=12ut⊤Ft(0)ut+O(∥ut∥23),\KL(\pi_{u}^{t}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}^{t})=\frac{1}{2}u_{t}^{\top}F_{t}(0)u_{t}+O(\|u_{t}\|_{2}^{3}), (7)

as ut→0u_{t}\to 0, where

Ft​(ut):=W⊤​(diag⁡(πut)−πut​(πut)⊤)​WF_{t}(u_{t}):=W^{\top}\bigl(\diag(\pi_{u}^{t})-\pi_{u}^{t}(\pi_{u}^{t})^{\top}\bigr)W (8)

is the Fisher information matrix with respect to utu_{t}.

The proof is given in Appendix B.3.

Since the token distribution depends on the prefix, the resulting Fisher matrix is prefix-dependent. To obtain fixed cost matrices required by (3), we average the Fisher matrix over reference-policy prefixes:

F¯t:=𝔼y<t∼πref​[Ft​(0)],ℰF¯​(u):=12​∑t=1Tut⊤​F¯t​ut.\bar{F}_{t}:=\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim\pi_{\text{ref}}}[F_{t}(0)],\qquad\mathcal{E}_{\bar{F}}(u):=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}u_{t}^{\top}\bar{F}_{t}u_{t}. (9)

Our proposed algorithm (MISVO) uses Σt=F¯t\Sigma_{t}=\bar{F}_{t}. This choice makes two approximations to the KL penalty in  (2): replacing each token-level KL by its quadratic expansion and replacing the steered prefix distribution by the reference distribution. We quantify their effects below.

Remark 1 (Variance interpretation).

The Fisher quadratic satisfies

ut⊤​Ft​(0)​ut=Vari∼πreft⁡[(W​ut)i].u_{t}^{\top}F_{t}(0)u_{t}=\operatorname{Var}_{i\sim\pi_{\text{ref}}^{t}}\bigl[(Wu_{t})_{i}\bigr]. (10)

Thus, the leading term of the token-level KL is one half of the variance of the logit perturbation. Unlike an isotropic penalty, this quadratic weights interventions by their effect on relative logits under the reference distribution. In particular, a constant shift of all logits incurs zero cost and leaves token probabilities unchanged.

We note that the approximation is local: neither the KL nor its Fisher quadratic globally bounds the other. Both are bounded above by 12​‖W​ut‖22≤12​σmax​(W)2​‖ut‖22\frac{1}{2}\|Wu_{t}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{1}{2}\sigma_{\max}(W)^{2}\|u_{t}\|_{2}^{2} (Appendix B.4).

4.2 Sequence-level KL gradient

To characterize the terms omitted by the quadratic surrogate, let K​(u):=ℰKL​(u)K(u):=\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{KL}}(u) and define the suffix log-ratio

ℓ>t​(y,u):=∑τ=t+1Tlog⁡πu​(yτ∣x,y<τ)πref​(yτ∣x,y<τ).\ell_{>t}(y;u):=\sum_{\tau=t+1}^{T}\log\frac{\pi_{u}(y_{\tau}\mid x,y_{<\tau})}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{\tau}\mid x,y_{<\tau})}.
Theorem 1 (Sequence-level KL gradient decomposition).

For every position tt,

∇utK​(u)\displaystyle\nabla_{u_{t}}K(u) =gtan​(u)+gtsuffix​(u),\displaystyle=g_{t}^{\mathrm{an}}(u)+g_{t}^{\mathrm{suffix}}(u), (11)
gtan​(u)\displaystyle g_{t}^{\mathrm{an}}(u) :=𝔼y<t∼πu​[Ft​(ut)]​ut,\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim\pi_{u}}[F_{t}(u_{t})]u_{t},
gtsuffix​(u)\displaystyle g_{t}^{\mathrm{suffix}}(u) :=𝔼y∼πu​[∇ut​log​πu​(yt∣x,y<t)​ℓ>t​(y,u)].\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{u}}\!\left[\nabla_{u_{t}}\log\pi_{u}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})\,\ell_{>t}(y;u)\right].

The proof is given in Appendix B.5. The decomposition separates the direct effect of utu_{t} on the current token distribution from its effect on future prefixes. At a fixed prefix, the token-level KL gradient is exactly Ft​(ut)​utF_{t}(u_{t})u_{t}; averaging over steered prefixes gives gtan​(u)g_{t}^{\mathrm{an}}(u). The suffix term captures the resulting change in future KL contributions through the prefix distribution.

Comparing (11) with the surrogate gradient F¯t​ut\bar{F}_{t}u_{t} reveals two sources of approximation error: replacing the iterate-dependent matrix 𝔼y<t∼πu​[Ft​(ut)]\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim\pi_{u}}[F_{t}(u_{t})] by the fixed reference matrix F¯t\bar{F}_{t}, and omitting the suffix score-function term. The next subsection bounds both errors to establish when the quadratic surrogate accurately approximates the full KL gradient.

Consider the three cost matrices

F~tu\displaystyle\tilde{F}_{t}^{u} :=𝔼y<t∼πu​[Ft​(ut)],\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim\pi_{u}}[F_{t}(u_{t})], (12)

The first gives the exact analytic term gtan​(u)=F~tu​utg_{t}^{\mathrm{an}}(u)=\tilde{F}_{t}^{u}u_{t}. The second evaluates the token Fisher at zero steering while retaining steered prefixes. The third also replaces the prefix distribution by the reference law.

The remaining discrepancy is the omitted suffix term.

Proposition 2 (Local bound on the suffix term).

For a fixed horizon TT and every t≤Tt\leq T,

gtsuffix​(u)=O⁡(‖u‖2)as ​u→0.g_{t}^{\mathrm{suffix}}(u)=O(\|u\|^{2})\qquad\text{as }u\to 0.

where the prefix dependence is shown explicitly. We reuse this estimate throughout optimization, so Fisher estimation requires no additional generations. The guarantees above concern the population matrices; the empirical gradient also contains the sampling error (F^t−F¯t)​ut(\widehat{F}_{t}-\bar{F}_{t})u_{t}.

4.4 Computational overhead

Over NN iterations with KK rollouts each, MISVO uses N​KNK generations and reward evaluations, matching the candidate budget of the BoN baseline. Its additional work includes reward-gradient estimation, Fisher estimation, and steering updates. The reward-gradient projections in (4) cost O⁡(N​K​T​V​d)O(NKTVd) in a direct implementation. We consider two ways to compute the regularizer gradient.

Explicit Fisher matrices.

Forming Ft=W⊤​Cπt​WF_{t}=W^{\top}C_{\pi^{t}}W costs O⁡(V​d2)O(Vd^{2}) per position and reference sample. Constructing all F^t\widehat{F}_{t} from the initial KK rollouts therefore costs O⁡(K​T​V​d2)O(KTVd^{2}) and requires O⁡(T​d2)O(Td^{2}) storage. Subsequent matrix–vector products cost O⁡(N​T​d2)O(NTd^{2}), giving a total of O⁡(K​T​V​d2+N​T​d2)O(KTVd^{2}+NTd^{2}). Reconstructing an iterate-dependent Fisher at every step would instead incur O⁡(N​K​T​V​d2)O(NKTVd^{2}) construction cost.

Matrix-free Fisher products.

The matrices need not be formed explicitly. For a token distribution pp and v=W​utv=Wu_{t},

Ft​ut=W⊤​Cp​v,Cp​v=p⊙v−p⁡(p⊤​v).F_{t}u_{t}=W^{\top}C_{p}v,\qquad C_{p}v=p\odot v-p(p^{\top}v).

Each product costs O⁡(V​d)O(Vd). Retaining SS reference hidden states per position permits reconstruction of the corresponding token probabilities and averaging of these products, with total cost O⁡(N​T​S​V​d)O(NTSVd) and retained-state storage O⁡(T​S​d)O(TSd). Our implementation uses this approach with S=KS=K initial rollouts. Vocabulary-sized intermediates require additional working memory; measured runtime and peak memory are reported in Appendix C.2.

5 Experiments

We evaluate MISVO on preference-based generation and code generation across four frozen models with approximately 1B–14B parameters. We compare reward at matched generation budgets, assess diversity and coherence, and measure distributional deviation on reference-policy prefixes.

5.1 Setup

Models.

We use four open-weight instruction-tuned base models with different architectures, hidden sizes, and parameter counts: LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct [4], Gemma3-4B-IT [39], Llama-3-8B-Instruct [5], and Phi-4 (14B) [1]. All four models are kept frozen throughout: only the per-token steering vectors u1:Tu_{1:T} are optimized, and the LM head (W,b)(W,b) is reused both for the forward pass and for the matrix-free Fisher–vector products in (8).

Tasks.

We consider two complementary alignment settings. (a) SHP [14]: open-ended preference-style generation. We sample 500500 prompts uniformly at random from the Stanford Human Preferences test set and score each generation with Skywork-Reward-V2-Qwen3-0.6B [28], a publicly released 0.60.6B-parameter preference reward model. We evaluate all four base models on this task. (b) MBPP+ [29]: program synthesis with an executable verifier. We use the first set of 120120 problems and reward each generation by the fraction of held-out unit tests it passes (in [0,1][0,1]); this provides a black-box, non-differentiable reward. We evaluate the three smaller models (LFM2.5-1.2B, Gemma3-4B, Llama-3-8B) on MBPP+. For both tasks, we cap generation at 512512 new tokens.

Best-so-far reporting.

Our primary metric is the highest reward among all K​NKN generations, where KK is the number of rollouts per step and NN is the number of optimization steps. MISVO and AISP generate candidates iteratively; Best-of-NN samples all candidates from the reference policy. This metric evaluates the response selected after search. We also report within-step mean and maximum rewards to assess the evolving steered policy.

Baselines.

Best-of-NN (top-pp) draws K⋅NK\cdot N candidate completions from the reference policy πref\pi_{\text{ref}} under the shared sampler and returns the highest-reward one; the budget is matched exactly to the total number of rollouts drawn by MISVO and AISP. AISP [19] performs sampling-based optimal control in pre-logit space using the importance-weighted update. We set σ2=0.5\sigma^{2}=0.5 and α=0.999\alpha=0.999 for their method. In line with the experimental results in [19], experiments with RE-Control [22] yielded inferior results, and due to computational limitations, we did not include it in our comparisons.

Our method.

MISVO uses the frozen-reference Fisher F¯t\bar{F}_{t} in (9). We estimate it from the first-step rollouts, for which u=0u=0, and reuse the estimate throughout optimization. These rollouts are included in the K​NKN budget.

Metrics.

We average all metrics over prompts. Reward is the Skywork score on SHP and the unit-test pass fraction on MBPP+, reported for the best response found during search. Diversity is ∏n∈{2,3,4}(1−repn)\prod_{n\in\{2,3,4\}}(1-\mathrm{rep}_{n}), where repn\mathrm{rep}_{n} is the fraction of repeated nn-grams within a response [19]. Coherence is the cosine similarity between SimCSE embeddings of the prompt and response [17]. The latter two metrics measure repetition and semantic relatedness; they do not establish distributional proximity, factual accuracy, or absence of reward exploitation.

Implementation details.

For each (model, task) pair we use the same MISVO and AISP hyperparameters across all prompts in the split. On both datasets we use K=16K=16, N=16N=16 for LFM2.5-1.2B and Gemma3-4B, and K=32K=32, N=32N=32 for Llama-3-8B and Phi-4; the learning rate is 0.10.1 and the regularization trade-off is λ=1\lambda=1. All runs use the Hugging Face transformers stack, fp16 weights for Llama-3 and bfloat16 for the others, and run on H200 GPUs. We report results as mean ±\pm standard deviation across 3 seeds.

5.2 Main results

Across both tasks (Tables 1 and 2), MISVO achieves the highest reported mean reward in six of the seven model–task settings. On SHP it improves over both BoN and AISP on three of the four models; the single exception is Llama-3-8B, where MISVO still improves over BoN but is overtaken by AISP. On MBPP+ MISVO leads on all three models, with the largest gain on the smallest.

Diversity and coherence scores remain close to those of BoN. These diagnostics suggest that reward gains are not accompanied by substantial deterioration in the measured properties, but do not establish proximity to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. Section 5.3 evaluates token-distribution deviation directly.

Reward trajectories.

Figure 2 reports the within-step mean reward, within-step maximum reward, and cumulative best reward for LFM2.5-1.2B on SHP. Within-step statistics use the KK rollouts from each iteration; the horizontal axis gives cumulative generations. Curves show means over three seeds, with shading indicating one standard deviation. Corresponding results for the other SHP models appear in Figures 3, 4, and 5. MISVO’s increasing within-step mean supports improvement in its sampling policy. AISP’s declining mean at later iterations is consistent with oversteering, although this metric alone does not identify the cause.

5.3 Direct measurement of policy deviation

To assess distributional deviation beyond generation-level diagnostics, we measure token-level KL on reference-policy prefixes. Given KK reference rollouts, define

KL^ref(u)=1K∑i=1K∑tKL(πu(⋅∣x,y<t(i))∥πref(⋅∣x,y<t(i))),y(i)∼πref\widehat{\text{KL}}_{\text{ref}}(u)\;=\;\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\sum_{t}\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y^{(i)}_{<t})\;\big\|\;\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x,y^{(i)}_{<t})\right),\quad y^{(i)}\sim\pi_{\text{ref}} (17)

where each token-level KL is computed over the full vocabulary. This estimates the sum of expected token KLs under reference-policy prefixes. It is distinct from the sequence-level KL in (2), whose expectations use steered-policy prefixes. The diagnostic measures deviation on reference contexts and does not capture all changes in prefix visitation induced by steering.

Table 3 reports results over 100 sampled prompts. MISVO attains the highest reported reward and lower reference-prefix KL than AISP and unregularized steering. The remaining regularizers do not exceed BoN in reward in this comparison. The direct-KL variant also has lower reward and higher reference-prefix KL than MISVO. These results describe the evaluated configurations; they do not establish a global reward–KL frontier or identify the cause of the direct-KL variant’s performance.

6 Conclusion

We introduced MISVO, which optimizes pre-logit interventions using a Fisher-quadratic penalty derived from local KL geometry. An exact sequence-level gradient decomposition and local error bounds establish first-order agreement between the frozen-Fisher gradient and the full KL gradient. Across seven model–task settings, MISVO achieves the highest reported mean reward in six, with diversity and coherence scores close to those of BoN.

Limitations.

The approximation is local and does not guarantee small sequence-level KL after large interventions. The empirical deviation metric uses reference-policy prefixes and therefore does not directly measure sequence-level KL. On SHP, the same reward model is used for optimization and primary evaluation, limiting conclusions about independent preference quality. MISVO also incurs iterative optimization overhead and, in our implementation, higher peak memory than the baselines. Its integration into high-throughput inference systems and the effects of more memory-efficient Fisher products remain directions for future work.

Appendix A Related Work

Training-time alignment.

RLHF optimizes model parameters using preference-derived rewards [12, 34, 37]. DPO expresses a KL-regularized preference objective as a classification loss [35]; other approaches modify the preference loss or feedback source [8, 15, 31, 9]. These methods produce model weights for deployment. MISVO instead optimizes interventions for the reward available at inference.

Prompt-based control.

Instructions, demonstrations, chain-of-thought prompting, and self-refinement guide generation through token inputs [11, 13, 42, 41, 30]. Their effectiveness depends on the model’s response to the supplied context. MISVO directly modifies the pre-logit representation and explicitly regularizes the resulting distributional change.

Output-level test-time alignment.

Best-of-NN selects the highest-reward completion among reference-policy samples [37, 10]. Guided decoding modifies token probabilities using reward models, value functions, or auxiliary scorers [21, 33, 25, 27, 44, 43]. MISVO instead optimizes a sequence of hidden-space interventions using a terminal reward.

Representation-level test-time alignment.

RE-Control uses a learned value function to guide hidden-state interventions [22]. AISP formulates pre-logit steering as sampling-based control and updates perturbations through importance-weighted reward evaluations [19]. BRT-Align uses latent backward reachability and a learned safety value function to determine when to intervene [20]. Static activation-steering methods estimate directions from offline data [38, 40, 36, 26, 46]; input-dependent variants also use optimal transport [2]. MISVO optimizes position-specific interventions against a runtime reward and regularizes them using the Fisher geometry of the output distribution. Its regularizer requires no auxiliary network, and its gradient agrees locally with the full sequence-level KL gradient to first order.

Proof.

Cp−Cq=diag⁡(p−q)−(p​p⊤−q​q⊤)C_{p}-C_{q}=\diag(p-q)-(pp^{\top}-qq^{\top}). For the diagonal piece, ‖diag⁡(p−q)‖2=‖p−q‖∞≤‖p−q‖2\|\diag(p-q)\|_{2}=\|p-q\|_{\infty}\leq\|p-q\|_{2}. For the rank-2 piece, write p​p⊤−q​q⊤=(p−q)​p⊤+q​(p−q)⊤pp^{\top}-qq^{\top}=(p-q)p^{\top}+q(p-q)^{\top}, so

‖p​p⊤−q​q⊤‖2≤‖p−q‖2​(‖p‖2+‖q‖2)≤ 2​‖p−q‖2,\|pp^{\top}-qq^{\top}\|_{2}\;\leq\;\|p-q\|_{2}(\|p\|_{2}+\|q\|_{2})\;\leq\;2\|p-q\|_{2},

using ‖p‖2,‖q‖2≤1\|p\|_{2},\|q\|_{2}\leq 1. Combining yields ‖Cp−Cq‖2≤3​‖p−q‖2\|C_{p}-C_{q}\|_{2}\leq 3\|p-q\|_{2}. ∎

Lemma 5 (Matrix-valued distance bound).

Let μ1,μ2\mu_{1},\mu_{2} be probability measures on a finite (or countable) set 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, and let M:𝒴→ℝn1×n2M:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} satisfy ‖M⁡(y)‖2≤B\|M(y)\|_{2}\leq B for all y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}. We have

‖𝔼μ1​[M]−𝔼μ2​[M]‖2≤B​‖μ1−μ2‖1.\big\|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{1}}[M]-\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{2}}[M]\big\|_{2}\;\leq\;B\,\|\mu_{1}-\mu_{2}\|_{1}.
Proof.

Set δ⁡(y):=μ1​(y)−μ2​(y)\delta(y):=\mu_{1}(y)-\mu_{2}(y), so that 𝔼μ1​[M]−𝔼μ2​[M]=∑y∈𝒴M⁡(y)​δ​(y)\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{1}}[M]-\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{2}}[M]=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}M(y)\,\delta(y). Applying the triangle inequality on the spectral norm,

‖∑y∈𝒴M⁡(y)​δ​(y)‖2≤∑y∈𝒴‖M⁡(y)‖2​|δ⁡(y)|≤B​∑y∈𝒴|δ⁡(y)|=B​‖μ1−μ2‖1.\Big\|\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}M(y)\,\delta(y)\Big\|_{2}\;\leq\;\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\|M(y)\|_{2}\,|\delta(y)|\;\leq\;B\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}|\delta(y)|\;=\;B\,\|\mu_{1}-\mu_{2}\|_{1}.

∎

B.2 Proof of the autoregressive chain rule

Proposition 3 (Eq. (2)).

For any two autoregressive policies πu,πref\pi_{u},\pi_{\text{ref}} over responses y=(y1,…,yT)y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{T}) given prompt xx,

KL(πu(⋅∣x)∥πref(⋅∣x))=∑t=1T𝔼y<t∼πu[KL(πu(⋅∣x,y<t)∥πref(⋅∣x,y<t))].\KL\!\big(\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)\big)\;=\;\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim\pi_{u}}\!\Big[\KL\!\big(\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\big)\Big]. (18)
Proof.

By the autoregressive factorization, log⁡πu​(y∣x)=∑t=1Tlog⁡πu​(yt∣x,y<t)\log\pi_{u}(y\mid x)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\pi_{u}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}) and similarly for πref\pi_{\text{ref}}. Therefore

KL(πu(⋅∣x)∥πref(⋅∣x))\displaystyle\KL(\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)) =∑yπu​(y∣x)​log⁡πu​(y∣x)πref​(y∣x)=∑yπu​(y∣x)​∑t=1Tlog⁡πu​(yt∣x,y<t)πref​(yt∣x,y<t)\displaystyle=\sum_{y}\pi_{u}(y\mid x)\log\frac{\pi_{u}(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}=\sum_{y}\pi_{u}(y\mid x)\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\frac{\pi_{u}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}
=∑t=1T∑yπu​(y∣x)​log⁡πu​(yt∣x,y<t)πref​(yt∣x,y<t).\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{y}\pi_{u}(y\mid x)\log\frac{\pi_{u}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}. (19)

The tt-th summand depends on yy only through y1:ty_{1:t}. Marginalizing yt+1:Ty_{t+1:T} and using πu(y1:t∣x)=πu(y<t∣x)πu(yt∣x,y<t)\pi_{u}(y_{1:t}\mid x)=\pi_{u}(y_{<t}\mid x)\,\pi_{u}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}),

∑yπu​(y∣x)​log⁡πu​(yt∣x,y<t)πref​(yt∣x,y<t)\displaystyle\sum_{y}\pi_{u}(y\mid x)\log\frac{\pi_{u}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})} =∑y<tπu​(y<t)​∑ytπu​(yt∣y<t)​log⁡πu​(yt∣y<t)πref​(yt∣y<t)\displaystyle=\sum_{y_{<t}}\pi_{u}(y_{<t})\sum_{y_{t}}\pi_{u}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})\log\tfrac{\pi_{u}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})}
=𝔼y<t∼πu[KL(πu(⋅∣y<t)∥πref(⋅∣y<t))],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim\pi_{u}}\!\big[\KL(\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid y_{<t})\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid y_{<t}))\big],

where we have suppressed the conditioning on xx for brevity. Summing over tt yields (18). ∎

B.3 Proof of Proposition 1

Fix two steering vectors u,vu,v at position tt (suppressing throughout this proof both the position subscript on the steering vectors and the position superscript on the per-position distributions, so we write u,vu,v for ut,vtu_{t},v_{t} and πu,πv\pi_{u},\pi_{v} for πut,πvt\pi_{u}^{t},\pi_{v}^{t}), let zu,zvz_{u},z_{v} denote the corresponding pre-softmax logits, and define δ:=zu−zv=W⁡(u−v)\delta:=z_{u}-z_{v}=W(u-v). KL(πu∥πv)=g(1)−g(0)=∫01τδ⊤Cπτδdτ.\KL(\pi_{u}\,\|\,\pi_{v})\;=\;g(1)-g(0)\;=\;\int_{0}^{1}\tau\,\delta^{\top}C_{\pi_{\tau}}\,\delta\,d\tau. (21)

|R|=|∫01τ​δ⊤​(Cπτ−Cπv)​δ​𝑑τ|≤|δ|∫0122⁡τ​‖Cπτ−Cπv‖2​𝑑τ.|R|\;=\;\Big|\int_{0}^{1}\tau\,\delta^{\top}(C_{\pi_{\tau}}-C_{\pi_{v}})\,\delta\,d\tau\Big|\;\leq\;\|\delta\|_{2}^{2}\int_{0}^{1}\tau\,\|C_{\pi_{\tau}}-C_{\pi_{v}}\|_{2}\,d\tau.

Proof.

+∑τ=1T𝔼y<τ∼πu[(∇utlogπu(y<τ∣x))𝒦τ(uτ;y<τ)].\displaystyle+\sum_{\tau=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{y_{<\tau}\sim\pi_{u}}\!\big[\big(\nabla_{u_{t}}\log\pi_{u}(y_{<\tau}\mid x)\big)\,\mathcal{K}_{\tau}(u_{\tau};y_{<\tau})\big]. (24)

𝔼y<τ∼πu(⋅∣x)[(∇utlogπu(yt∣x,y<t))𝒦τ(uτ;y<τ)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{y_{<\tau}\sim\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x)}\!\Big[\big(\nabla_{u_{t}}\log\pi_{u}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})\big)\,\mathcal{K}_{\tau}(u_{\tau};y_{<\tau})\Big] =\displaystyle\;=\;
𝔼y≤t∼πu(⋅∣x)[(∇utlogπu(yt∣x,y<t))\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{y_{\leq t}\sim\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x)}\!\bigg[\big(\nabla_{u_{t}}\log\pi_{u}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})\big)
×𝔼yt+1:τ−1∼πu(⋅∣x,y≤t)[𝒦τ(uτ;y<τ)]].\displaystyle\times\,\mathbb{E}_{y_{t+1:\tau-1}\sim\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{\leq t})}\!\big[\mathcal{K}_{\tau}(u_{\tau};y_{<\tau})\big]\bigg].

Summing over τ≥t+2\tau\geq t+2, combining with the τ=t+1\tau=t+1 term, and exchanging the finite sum with the outer expectation,

𝒯(u)=𝔼y≤t∼πu(⋅∣x)[(∇utlogπu(yt∣x,y<t))S(y≤t;u)],\mathcal{T}(u)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{y_{\leq t}\sim\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x)}\!\Big[\big(\nabla_{u_{t}}\log\pi_{u}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})\big)\,S(y_{\leq t};u)\Big], (29)

where we have introduced the auxiliary quantity

S(y≤t;u):=𝒦t+1(ut+1;y<t+1)+∑τ=t+2T𝔼yt+1:τ−1∼πu(⋅∣x,y≤t)[𝒦τ(uτ;y<τ)].S(y_{\leq t};u)\;:=\;\mathcal{K}_{t+1}(u_{t+1};y_{<t+1})\;+\;\sum_{\tau=t+2}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{y_{t+1:\tau-1}\sim\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{\leq t})}\!\big[\mathcal{K}_{\tau}(u_{\tau};y_{<\tau})\big]. (30)

(c) Identifying S⁡(y≤t,u)S(y_{\leq t};u) as the conditional suffix KL. Fix y≤ty_{\leq t} and apply the autoregressive chain rule of Appendix B.2 to the conditional sequence laws πu(⋅∣x,y≤t)\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{\leq t}) and πref(⋅∣x,y≤t)\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x,y_{\leq t}) over the suffix variable y>t=(yt+1,…,yT)y_{>t}=(y_{t+1},\ldots,y_{T}). The first chain-rule term (corresponding to the absolute position τ=t+1\tau=t+1) is the per-position KL at position t+1t+1 given y≤ty_{\leq t}, with no further conditional averaging; the remaining terms (τ≥t+2\tau\geq t+2) involve genuine conditional expectations over intermediate suffix tokens. We have

KL(πu(⋅∣x,y≤t)∥πref(⋅∣x,y≤t))=𝒦t+1​(ut+1,y<t+1)+∑τ=t+2T𝔼yt+1:τ−1∼πu(⋅∣x,y≤t)[𝒦τ(uτ;y<τ)]=S⁡(y≤t,u).\displaystyle\begin{split}\KL\!\big(\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{\leq t})\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x,y_{\leq t})\big)&\!=\!\mathcal{K}_{t+1}(u_{t+1};y_{<t+1})\\ &\quad+\sum_{\tau=t+2}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{y_{t+1:\tau-1}\sim\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{\leq t})}\!\big[\mathcal{K}_{\tau}(u_{\tau};y_{<\tau})\big]\;\\ &=\;S(y_{\leq t};u).\end{split} (31)

On the other hand, expanding the same conditional KL directly as an expectation of a sum of log-ratios under πu(⋅∣x,y≤t)\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{\leq t}),

KL(πu(⋅∣x,y≤t)∥πref(⋅∣x,y≤t))=𝔼y>t∼πu(⋅∣x,y≤t)[∑τ>tlogπu​(yτ∣x,y<τ)πref​(yτ∣x,y<τ)]=𝔼y>t∼πu(⋅∣x,y≤t)[ℓ>t(y)],\displaystyle\begin{split}\KL\!\big(\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{\leq t})\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x,y_{\leq t})\big)\;&=\;\mathbb{E}_{y_{>t}\sim\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{\leq t})}\!\Big[\sum_{\tau>t}\log\tfrac{\pi_{u}(y_{\tau}\mid x,y_{<\tau})}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{\tau}\mid x,y_{<\tau})}\Big]\\ &=\;\mathbb{E}_{y_{>t}\sim\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{\leq t})}\!\big[\ell_{>t}(y)\big],\end{split} (32)

where the last equality uses ℓ>t​(y)=∑τ>tlog⁡πu​(yτ∣x,y<τ)πref​(yτ∣x,y<τ)\ell_{>t}(y)=\sum_{\tau>t}\log\tfrac{\pi_{u}(y_{\tau}\mid x,y_{<\tau})}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{\tau}\mid x,y_{<\tau})} (and note that ℓ>t​(y)\ell_{>t}(y) depends on yy only through its suffix y>ty_{>t} once y≤ty_{\leq t} is fixed). Combining (31) and (32),

S(y≤t;u)=𝔼y>t∼πu(⋅∣x,y≤t)[ℓ>t(y)].S(y_{\leq t};u)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{y_{>t}\sim\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{\leq t})}\!\big[\ell_{>t}(y)\big]. (33)

Combining the pieces. Substituting (33) into (29) and merging the outer expectation over y≤t∼πu(⋅∣x)y_{\leq t}\sim\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x) with the inner expectation over y>t|y≤ty_{>t}\mid y_{\leq t} into a single expectation over y∼πu(⋅∣x)y\sim\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x), we have

𝒯(u)=𝔼y∼πu(⋅∣x)[(∇utlogπu(yt∣x,y<t))ℓ>t(y)].\mathcal{T}(u)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x)}\!\Big[\big(\nabla_{u_{t}}\log\pi_{u}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})\big)\,\ell_{>t}(y)\Big]. (34)

This is the suffix score-function term in Theorem 1. Combining (34) with the analytic term established in Step 3 yields (11) and completes the proof. ∎

B.6 Proof of Theorem 2

Proof.

Step 1: bounding ‖Ft​(ut)−Ft​(0)‖2\|F_{t}(u_{t})-F_{t}(0)\|_{2} pointwise in y<ty_{<t}. By definition Ft​(ut)−Ft​(0)=W⊤​(Cπut−Cπreft)​WF_{t}(u_{t})-F_{t}(0)=W^{\top}(C_{\pi_{u}^{t}}-C_{\pi_{\text{ref}}^{t}})W, so

‖Ft​(ut)−Ft​(0)‖2≤σmax​(W)2​‖Cπut−Cπreft‖2≤ 3​σmax​(W)2​‖πut−πreft‖2,\|F_{t}(u_{t})-F_{t}(0)\|_{2}\;\leq\;\sigma_{\max}(W)^{2}\,\|C_{\pi_{u}^{t}}-C_{\pi_{\text{ref}}^{t}}\|_{2}\;\leq\;3\sigma_{\max}(W)^{2}\,\|\pi_{u}^{t}-\pi_{\text{ref}}^{t}\|_{2}, (35)

using Lemma 4. By Lemma 3, ‖πut−πreft‖2≤‖δ‖2=‖W​ut‖2≤σmax​(W)​‖ut‖2\|\pi_{u}^{t}-\pi_{\text{ref}}^{t}\|_{2}\leq\|\delta\|_{2}=\|Wu_{t}\|_{2}\leq\sigma_{\max}(W)\|u_{t}\|_{2}. Substituting,

‖Ft​(ut)−Ft​(0)‖2≤ 3​σmax​(W)3​‖ut‖2=:C1​‖ut‖2,\|F_{t}(u_{t})-F_{t}(0)\|_{2}\;\leq\;3\sigma_{\max}(W)^{3}\,\|u_{t}\|_{2}\;=:\;C_{1}\,\|u_{t}\|_{2}, (36)

with C1=3​σmax​(W)3C_{1}=3\sigma_{\max}(W)^{3}. This bound is uniform in y<ty_{<t}.

Step 2: bounding trajectory drift. Define the (random) matrix M⁡(y<t):=Ft​(0)M(y_{<t}):=F_{t}(0) as a function of the context y<ty_{<t} (through hth_{t}). We bound

‖F¯tu−F¯t‖2=‖𝔼y<t∼πu​[M]−𝔼y<t∼πref​[M]‖2.\big\|\bar{F}_{t}^{u}-\bar{F}_{t}\big\|_{2}\;=\;\big\|\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim\pi_{u}}[M]-\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim\pi_{\text{ref}}}[M]\big\|_{2}. (37)

We first bound ‖M⁡(y<t)‖2≤σmax​(W)2\|M(y_{<t})\|_{2}\leq\sigma_{\max}(W)^{2} uniformly, since ‖Cp‖2≤1\|C_{p}\|_{2}\leq 1 (Lemma 2). Next, by Lemma 5, we have

‖𝔼μ1​[M]−𝔼μ2​[M]‖2≤σmax​(W)2​‖μ1−μ2‖1.\big\|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{1}}[M]-\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{2}}[M]\big\|_{2}\;\leq\;\sigma_{\max}(W)^{2}\,\|\mu_{1}-\mu_{2}\|_{1}. (38)

It remains to bound ∥πu(⋅∣x)−πref(⋅∣x)∥1\|\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x)-\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)\|_{1} restricted to the first t−1t-1 coordinates (the trajectory law governing y<ty_{<t}). We use the following sequential coupling argument.

Lemma 6.

The trajectory laws of πu\pi_{u} and πref\pi_{\text{ref}} restricted to y<ty_{<t} satisfy

‖πu​(y<t∣x)−πref​(y<t∣x)‖1≤Ltraj​∑τ<t‖uτ‖2,Ltraj=V​σmax​(W).\big\|\pi_{u}(y_{<t}\mid x)-\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{<t}\mid x)\big\|_{1}\;\leq\;L_{\mathrm{traj}}\sum_{\tau<t}\|u_{\tau}\|_{2},\qquad L_{\mathrm{traj}}=\sqrt{V}\,\sigma_{\max}(W).
Proof.

The proof has two parts: we first establish a sequential decomposition of the ℓ1\ell_{1} distance for autoregressive laws, and then apply it to μ=πu(⋅∣x)\mu=\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x) and ν=πref(⋅∣x)\nu=\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x) restricted to y<ty_{<t}.

Step A: For any two autoregressive laws μ,ν\mu,\nu on y<t=(y1,…,yt−1)y_{<t}=(y_{1},\dots,y_{t-1}),

∥μ−ν∥1≤∑τ<t𝔼y<τ∼μ[∥μ(⋅∣y<τ)−ν(⋅∣y<τ)∥1].\|\mu-\nu\|_{1}\;\leq\;\sum_{\tau<t}\mathbb{E}_{y_{<\tau}\sim\mu}\!\Big[\|\mu(\cdot\mid y_{<\tau})-\nu(\cdot\mid y_{<\tau})\|_{1}\Big]. (39)

The idea is to interpolate from ν\nu to μ\mu by switching one conditional factor at a time. Define, for 0≤τ≤t−10\leq\tau\leq t-1, the intermediate distribution

Pτ​(y<t):=∏r=1τμ⁡(yr∣y<r)​∏r=τ+1t−1ν⁡(yr∣y<r),P_{\tau}(y_{<t})\;:=\;\prod_{r=1}^{\tau}\mu(y_{r}\mid y_{<r})\,\prod_{r=\tau+1}^{t-1}\nu(y_{r}\mid y_{<r}),

with the convention that empty products equal 11. Then P0=νP_{0}=\nu, Pt−1=μP_{t-1}=\mu, and

μ−ν=Pt−1−P0=∑τ=1t−1(Pτ−Pτ−1).\mu-\nu\;=\;P_{t-1}-P_{0}\;=\;\sum_{\tau=1}^{t-1}\bigl(P_{\tau}-P_{\tau-1}\bigr).

For each 1≤τ≤t−11\leq\tau\leq t-1, only the τ\tau-th factor differs between PτP_{\tau} and Pτ−1P_{\tau-1}, so

Pτ​(y<t)−Pτ−1​(y<t)=μ⁡(y<τ)​[μ⁡(yτ∣y<τ)−ν⁡(yτ∣y<τ)]​∏r=τ+1t−1ν⁡(yr∣y<r),P_{\tau}(y_{<t})-P_{\tau-1}(y_{<t})\;=\;\mu(y_{<\tau})\,\big[\mu(y_{\tau}\mid y_{<\tau})-\nu(y_{\tau}\mid y_{<\tau})\big]\,\prod_{r=\tau+1}^{t-1}\nu(y_{r}\mid y_{<r}),

where μ⁡(y<τ):=∏r=1τ−1μ⁡(yr∣y<r)\mu(y_{<\tau}):=\prod_{r=1}^{\tau-1}\mu(y_{r}\mid y_{<r}) is the marginal of μ\mu on the first τ−1\tau-1 coordinates. Taking absolute values and summing over y<ty_{<t}, the leading μ\mu-product and trailing ν\nu-product are non-negative and the trailing one marginalizes to 11 for any fixed y<τ+1y_{<\tau+1} (since ∑yτ+1:t−1∏r=τ+1t−1ν(yr∣y<r)=1\sum_{y_{\tau+1:t-1}}\prod_{r=\tau+1}^{t-1}\nu(y_{r}\mid y_{<r})=1). Hence

‖Pτ−Pτ−1‖1\displaystyle\|P_{\tau}-P_{\tau-1}\|_{1} =∑y<τμ⁡(y<τ)​∑yτ|μ⁡(yτ∣y<τ)−ν⁡(yτ∣y<τ)|\displaystyle=\;\sum_{y_{<\tau}}\mu(y_{<\tau})\sum_{y_{\tau}}\big|\mu(y_{\tau}\mid y_{<\tau})-\nu(y_{\tau}\mid y_{<\tau})\big|
=𝔼y<τ∼μ[∥μ(⋅∣y<τ)−ν(⋅∣y<τ)∥1].\displaystyle=\;\,\mathbb{E}_{y_{<\tau}\sim\mu}\!\Big[\|\mu(\cdot\mid y_{<\tau})-\nu(\cdot\mid y_{<\tau})\|_{1}\Big].

Applying the triangle inequality to ‖μ−ν‖1\|\mu-\nu\|_{1},

∥μ−ν∥1≤∑τ=1t−1∥Pτ−Pτ−1∥1=∑τ<t𝔼y<τ∼μ[∥μ(⋅∣y<τ)−ν(⋅∣y<τ)∥1],\|\mu-\nu\|_{1}\;\leq\;\sum_{\tau=1}^{t-1}\|P_{\tau}-P_{\tau-1}\|_{1}\;=\;\sum_{\tau<t}\mathbb{E}_{y_{<\tau}\sim\mu}\!\Big[\|\mu(\cdot\mid y_{<\tau})-\nu(\cdot\mid y_{<\tau})\|_{1}\Big],

which is (39).

Step B: application to πu\pi_{u} and πref\pi_{\text{ref}}. Apply (39) with μ=πu(⋅∣x)\mu=\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x) and ν=πref(⋅∣x)\nu=\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x). At each position τ<t\tau<t, since steering is applied only at the pre-logit stage, πu(⋅∣x,y<τ)\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<\tau}) and πref(⋅∣x,y<τ)\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<\tau}) share the same hidden state hτ=hτ​(x,y<τ)h_{\tau}=h_{\tau}(x,y_{<\tau}), and the per-step logit perturbation is δτ=W​uτ\delta_{\tau}=Wu_{\tau}. By Lemma 3, we have

∥πu(⋅∣x,y<τ)−πref(⋅∣x,y<τ)∥1≤V∥Wuτ∥2≤Vσmax(W)∥uτ∥2.\|\pi_{u}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<\tau})-\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<\tau})\|_{1}\;\leq\;\sqrt{V}\,\|Wu_{\tau}\|_{2}\;\leq\;\sqrt{V}\,\sigma_{\max}(W)\,\|u_{\tau}\|_{2}.

This bound is uniform in y<τy_{<\tau}, so taking the expectation under πu\pi_{u} does not enlarge it. Substituting into (39),

‖πu​(y<t∣x)−πref​(y<t∣x)‖1≤∑τ<tV​σmax​(W)​‖uτ‖2=V​σmax​(W)​∑τ<t‖uτ‖2,\big\|\pi_{u}(y_{<t}\mid x)-\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{<t}\mid x)\big\|_{1}\;\leq\;\sum_{\tau<t}\sqrt{V}\,\sigma_{\max}(W)\,\|u_{\tau}\|_{2}\;=\;\sqrt{V}\,\sigma_{\max}(W)\sum_{\tau<t}\|u_{\tau}\|_{2},

which is the claim with Ltraj=V​σmax​(W)L_{\mathrm{traj}}=\sqrt{V}\,\sigma_{\max}(W). ∎

Combining (38) with Lemma 6:

∥F¯tu−F¯t∥2≤σmax(W)2⋅Ltraj∑τ<t∥uτ∥2=:C2∑τ<t∥uτ∥2,\|\bar{F}_{t}^{u}-\bar{F}_{t}\|_{2}\;\leq\;\sigma_{\max}(W)^{2}\cdot L_{\mathrm{traj}}\sum_{\tau<t}\|u_{\tau}\|_{2}\;=:\;C_{2}\sum_{\tau<t}\|u_{\tau}\|_{2}, (40)

with C2=V​σmax​(W)3C_{2}=\sqrt{V}\,\sigma_{\max}(W)^{3}.

Step 3: bounding ‖F~tu−F¯tu‖2\|\tilde{F}_{t}^{u}-\bar{F}_{t}^{u}\|_{2}. By definition,

F~tu−F¯tu=𝔼y<t∼πu​[Ft​(ut)−Ft​(0)],\tilde{F}_{t}^{u}-\bar{F}_{t}^{u}\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim\pi_{u}}\!\big[F_{t}(u_{t})-F_{t}(0)\big],

and Step 1 gives ‖Ft​(ut)−Ft​(0)‖2≤C1​‖ut‖2\|F_{t}(u_{t})-F_{t}(0)\|_{2}\leq C_{1}\|u_{t}\|_{2} pointwise in y<ty_{<t}. Using Jensen’s inequality (‖𝔼⁡[X]‖2≤𝔼​‖X‖2\|\mathbb{E}[X]\|_{2}\leq\mathbb{E}\|X\|_{2}) we get

‖F~tu−F¯tu‖2≤C1​‖ut‖2.\|\tilde{F}_{t}^{u}-\bar{F}_{t}^{u}\|_{2}\;\leq\;C_{1}\,\|u_{t}\|_{2}. (41)

Step 4: gradient equivalence. Considering the norm of the gradient differences of the regularizers, using  (40) and (41), we have:

‖F¯tu​ut−F¯t​ut‖2\displaystyle\|\bar{F}_{t}^{u}u_{t}-\bar{F}_{t}u_{t}\|_{2}\; ≤C2​‖ut‖2​∑τ<t‖uτ‖2=O⁡(‖u‖2),\displaystyle\leq\;C_{2}\,\|u_{t}\|_{2}\sum_{\tau<t}\|u_{\tau}\|_{2}\;=\;O(\|u\|^{2}), (42)
‖F~tu​ut−F¯tu​ut‖2\displaystyle\|\tilde{F}_{t}^{u}u_{t}-\bar{F}_{t}^{u}u_{t}\|_{2}\; ≤C1​‖ut‖22=O⁡(‖u‖2).\displaystyle\leq\;C_{1}\,\|u_{t}\|_{2}^{2}\;=\;O(\|u\|^{2}). (43)

By the triangle inequality, ‖F~tu​ut−F¯t​ut‖2=O⁡(‖u‖2)\|\tilde{F}_{t}^{u}u_{t}-\bar{F}_{t}u_{t}\|_{2}=O(\|u\|^{2}) as well.

∎

B.7 Proof of Proposition 2

In this proof, 𝒦⁡(u)=K⁡(u)\mathcal{K}(u)=K(u), and uu is identified with its vectorization in ℝT​d\mathbb{R}^{Td}.

Proof.

Step 1: the sequence score is block separable and collapses to position tt. Applying (27) with τ=T+1\tau=T+1 (so that y<τ=yy_{<\tau}=y) gives ∇ut​log​πu​(y∣x)=∇ut​log​πu​(yt∣x,y<t)\nabla_{u_{t}}\log\pi_{u}(y\mid x)=\nabla_{u_{t}}\log\pi_{u}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}): only the position-tt factor of the autoregressive product depends on utu_{t}, because steering enters at the pre-logit stage and the hidden states hτ​(x,y<τ)h_{\tau}(x,y_{<\tau}) are uu-independent. St​(y,u)\displaystyle S_{t}(y;u) :=W⊤​(eyt−πut),\displaystyle:=W^{\top}\big(e_{y_{t}}-\pi_{u}^{t}\big),

and abbreviate its value at the origin by S⁡(y):=S⁡(y,0)S(y):=S(y;0), with blocks St​(y)=W⊤​(eyt−πreft)S_{t}(y)=W^{\top}(e_{y_{t}}-\pi_{\text{ref}}^{t}). We suppress the argument yy when no confusion arises and write SS, StS_{t}.

In (II)(\mathrm{II}), substituting (47) for the left factor and (46) for the right factor,

𝔼πref​[Sτ∣y<τ]=W⊤​(πrefτ−πrefτ)= 0.\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\text{ref}}}\!\big[S_{\tau}\mid y_{<\tau}\big]\;=\;W^{\top}\big(\pi_{\text{ref}}^{\tau}-\pi_{\text{ref}}^{\tau}\big)\;=\;0.

𝔼πref​[Sτ​Sτ⊤∣y<τ]=W⊤​Cπrefτ​W=Fτ​(0),\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\text{ref}}}\!\big[S_{\tau}S_{\tau}^{\top}\mid y_{<\tau}\big]\;=\;W^{\top}\,C_{\pi_{\text{ref}}^{\tau}}\,W\;=\;F_{\tau}(0),

by the definition (8) of Fτ​(⋅)F_{\tau}(\cdot). Taking the outer expectation over y<τ∼πrefy_{<\tau}\sim\pi_{\text{ref}} and invoking (9),

𝔼πref​[Sτ​Sτ⊤]=𝔼y<τ∼πref​[Fτ​(0)]=F¯τ,\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\text{ref}}}\!\big[S_{\tau}S_{\tau}^{\top}\big]\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{y_{<\tau}\sim\pi_{\text{ref}}}\!\big[F_{\tau}(0)\big]\;=\;\bar{F}_{\tau},

which is exactly the initial Fisher regularizer. Combining with Step 3,

∇2𝒦​(0)=blkdiag⁡(F¯1,…,F¯T).\nabla^{2}\mathcal{K}(0)\;=\;\operatorname{blkdiag}\big(\bar{F}_{1},\dots,\bar{F}_{T}\big). (49)

∇ut𝒦(u)=F¯tut+O(∥u∥2),t=1,…,T.\nabla_{u_{t}}\mathcal{K}(u)\;=\;\bar{F}_{t}\,u_{t}\;+\;O(\|u\|^{2}),\qquad t=1,\dots,T. (50)

Appendix C Further Experimental Results

C.1 Ablation: Fisher surrogates

We compare the Fisher surrogates {F¯t,F¯tu,F~tu}\{\bar{F}_{t},\bar{F}_{t}^{u},\tilde{F}_{t}^{u}\} and a KL-regularized variant on LFM2.5-1.2B with SHP, holding the remaining hyperparameters at their main-experiment values.

Table 4 reports reward differences of at most 0.340.34 and diversity/coherence differences of at most 0.0130.013 among the Fisher variants. The frozen-reference surrogate has the highest reported reward in this setting. The variants’ similar performance is compatible with their local first-order equivalence, but does not establish that the experiments remain in the asymptotic regime. The KL-regularized variant has lower reported reward.

C.2 Runtime and memory

We profile each method on two models using one NVIDIA H200 NVL. After loading the language and reward models, we process five warmup prompts followed by ten timed prompts, sequentially. CUDA events bracket each per-prompt invocation, including sampling, reward scoring, optimization, and response selection. Table 5 reports per-prompt latency, generation throughput, and peak GPU memory on SHP with a 512-token generation cap. BoN is fastest on both models; AISP and MISVO interleave generation with scoring and updates.

MISVO retains reference hidden states from the initial rollouts and uses vocabulary-sized intermediates for Fisher–vector products. These contribute to its higher peak memory. Chunked products may reduce working memory, but we do not evaluate them here.

The measurements use single-prompt batches: KK rollouts per iteration for AISP/MISVO and K​NKN candidates for BoN. Cross-prompt batching may change throughput and is outside this profiling protocol.

Appendix D Relation to per-prompt adapter fitting

Per-prompt low-rank adaptation (LoRA) offers another form of test-time reward optimization. Its cost depends on adapter rank, placement, and the gradients required for the adapted modules. Pre-logit steering confines optimization to additive interventions at the frozen LM head and retains a shared set of model weights.

Our experiments compare candidate selection and pre-logit steering at matched rollout counts. This isolates performance at a common sampling budget but does not equalize wall-clock cost or memory. A comparison with per-prompt LoRA under both rollout and runtime budgets would broaden the evaluation. We leave this comparison to future work and make no claim that steering is preferable to adapter fitting.
